title: Why Japan declined to attach an inflation number to price stability in 2000
summary: The Board’s October report sets out what it wanted monetary policy to preserve. Firms and households should be able to make spending, saving and investment decisions without having to anticipate disruptive changes in purchasing power. The Board decided that a durable numerical definition would be a poor guide in the Japanese economy it faced at the time. It chose to disclose the evidence it used to judge price stability and to publish a longer-horizon outlook with individual members’ forecasts. The numbers in that future outlook would describe possible economic outcomes. They would not specify a policy objective.

Sections 1–2 explain why the distinction matters. Stable prices make a change in relative prices easier to interpret, reduce uncertainty for people entering long-term contracts, and limit unexpected transfers between debtors and creditors. Policy can influence aggregate demand and expectations over time, but the lag and strength of its effects are uncertain. The report gives two reasons easing can have particular difficulty arresting deflation. Once nominal rates reach zero in the framework it uses, falling inflation expectations raise real rates. Separately, banks facing impaired capital can restrain lending while highly indebted firms or households cut spending. The report presents these as mechanisms, without estimating how much either explained current conditions.

Section 3 considers a small positive inflation buffer. New products, changes in quality and households switching to cheaper items can introduce a gap between a measured index and the economic cost of living. A positive measured number could thus coexist with underlying price stability. A buffer could also reduce exposure to the zero-rate constraint. The Board found the magnitude and persistence of index bias hard to estimate. Members also questioned how much downward wage rigidity contributed in Japan and how much protection a small positive buffer would buy. Several thought a positive measured rate merited study over the longer run. The report does not turn that view into a numerical target.

The origin of a price change also affects its interpretation. Weak spending can depress both prices and activity. Higher productivity can lower prices while encouraging new demand and investment, even as firms in some sectors lose profits. The Board uses Japan’s 1996 experience to illustrate the distinction. Its report cites economic growth of around 5 percent alongside the largest decline of the 1990s in the GDP deflator. It describes IT-related investment as supporting growth. It does not establish which share of the deflator decline came from any one cause. The account also recognises the opposite risk. A rise in imported oil prices might initially be a relative-price shock but could take on broader significance if domestic inflation expectations changed.

The historical charts show why the choice of indicator matters. Chart 3 reports average Japanese all-items consumer inflation of 0.5 percent in 1996–99, compared with 1.8 percent for the weighted G7 aggregate. Japanese wholesale prices fell by 1.0 percent per year on average in that period. The G7 producer or wholesale measure uses a different aggregation rule, so the two cross-country panels cannot be compared as though their weights were identical. Chart 4 examines the late 1980s. The report points to growth of around 5 percent in 1987 and 1988 while consumer inflation stayed between zero and 1 percent and wholesale prices declined year on year. Movements in equities and land conveyed a different picture of financial vulnerability. The Board regarded asset prices as evidence about future spending and credit risks, while rejecting them as a direct target.

Section 4 sets out three practical questions. What explains the behaviour of different price measures? Is the prevailing degree of stability sustainable? Is it consistent with sound economic and financial development? CPI, wholesale prices, corporate service prices and the GDP deflator differ in coverage. They also arrive at different times. The report notes a delay of over two months for the deflator and substantial differences between some preliminary and final estimates. The Board would check labour utilisation, wages, business surveys, the exchange rate and market prices alongside inflation. It cautions that estimates of spare capacity become less reliable during structural change and that thin markets reduce the value of prices as signals of expectations.

Finally, section 5 explains what the planned outlook adds to the existing monthly view. The monthly assessment focuses mainly on the likely course of the economy over the next few months. The longer-horizon publication would consider consequential risks even where their probability appeared low. Members could differ in assumptions and models. The report notes that the period over which a forecast is reasonably reliable can be shorter than the time policy takes to influence activity and prices. A missed forecast, a dissenting endpoint or a volatile market rate therefore needs an economic interpretation before it can indicate how the Board is likely to vote.

questions.question: Could real-time data distinguish weak demand from productivity-driven price declines?
questions.detail: Build a historical panel using the initial releases of sales, output, investment, profits, wages and sector-level prices. Compare patterns in sectors exposed to technology or deregulation with those more exposed to domestic demand. Run the same test using revised data to measure how much clarity only became available later.

questions.question: How much would the choice of inflation measure have changed a policy signal?
questions.detail: Date each index by its actual release, compare its coverage and separately track revisions to the GDP deflator. Test whether apparent differences survive a common information cutoff. For cross-country comparisons reproduce the report’s weighting conventions and distinguish wholesale from consumer prices.

questions.question: Could financial indicators identify vulnerabilities while measured CPI stayed quiet?
questions.detail: Follow credit volumes, equity and land values, bank balance sheets and measures of market liquidity alongside the price indexes. Compare an early-warning rule using only consumer prices with one that also uses those financial measures. A useful warning should precede deterioration and avoid false signals in calmer periods.

questions.question: Did the new outlook change investors’ understanding of policy conditionality?
questions.detail: Compare rate expectations and forecast dispersion around the methodology announcement and the first actual publication. Code whether subsequent reporting interpreted forecasts as contingent estimates or targets. Co-released policy documents and the liquidity of the instruments limit what prices alone can establish.
